title: Free tool strategy: using engineering as marketing to earn leads, links and traffic
summary: Corey's playbook for planning free tools (calculators, generators, graders) as an acquisition channel. Pick a real problem adjacent to your product, ship a tiny MVP, gate lightly, and judge it by leads and conversion in your own funnel, not visits.

principles.text: Turn a capability others monetize into a free acquisition channel.
principles.quote: take a capability others monetize and build a free version as an acquisition channel. Unsplash gave away the stock photos Getty sold — and Getty acquired it.

principles.text: A good free tool solves a real problem and sits next to your product, with a natural path from tool to product.
principles.quote:
Related to what you sell
- Natural path from tool to product
- Educates on problem you solve

principles.text: Keep it simple: one job, low friction, immediate value.
principles.quote:
Does one thing well
- Low friction to use
- Immediate value

principles.text: Ideate from what your audience Googles, finds tedious, or needs before buying.
principles.quote: What problems does your audience Google?** - Search query research, common questions

principles.text: Ship a minimum viable tool and skip accounts, saving results, and polish at first.
principles.quote: Core functionality only—does the one thing, works reliably

principles.text: Don't over-engineer; validate demand first, then invest. Measure leads and conversion, not vanity traffic.
principles.quote: Unsplash started as a Tumblr blog with Dropbox links, then invested in a custom site after demand emerged. Scope to one useful job and test it with your audience.
